blocks.h: Why count instead of walking k steps?

Flip the DP (Dynamic Programming): instead of 'moves for n floors', compute 'floors for m moves'
Drop an egg: if it breaks, `dp[e-1]` floors below remain with one fewer egg; if it survives, `dp[e]` floors above remain with the same eggs; plus the floor tested

p: `k = 2` eggs, `n = 6` floors. After each move the table shows how many floors each egg count can cover:
After 3 moves two eggs cover 6 floors, so the answer is 3. With one egg it takes `n` moves (5 for 5 floors), and with 3 eggs and 14 floors it takes 4.

The direct DP `f(k, n)` tries every first floor, costing O(k · n²) (or O(k · n log n) with binary search). Counting how many floors a number of moves can cover gives a recurrence with no search at all, and the number of moves is at most `n` (and usually tiny, about log n for many eggs).

blocks.h: Why do swaps equal the zeros in the window?
p: If we choose a window of length `w` as the final home of all ones, every zero inside it must trade places with a one outside (there are exactly as many ones outside as zeros inside). blocks.h: Why generate palindromes instead of scanning numbers?

bullets: Time: roughly O(P · log) for P decimal palindromes generated until n matches are found.

2081.takeaway: k-mirror numbers: generate decimal palindromes in increasing order from their halves and keep those that are also palindromes in base k.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Upper bound: total energy shared by `n` computers
Even sharing is the best conceivable
A battery can supply at most `mid` minutes toward a target of `mid` minutes (it cannot power two computers at the same time, and we only need `mid` from each computer)
Enough usable energy to run `n` computers for `mid` minutes
Search for the LAST feasible value; upper midpoint prevents an infinite loop

blocks.h: Why can we ignore the swapping schedule?
p: Batteries can be swapped at any integer minute, and swapping is free. So the question is only whether the total usable energy can be divided so that each of the `n` computers gets `mid` minutes, with no battery used by two computers at once. Capping each battery at `mid` guarantees that, and the condition `sum ≥ n·mid` is then sufficient.

bullets: Time: O(m log(sum / n)) for m batteries.

2141.takeaway: Maximum run time of n computers: binary search the time; feasible if the sum of min(battery, time) is at least n × time.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The odd digits and the even digits, each sorted in DESCENDING order
Swaps are allowed only between digits of the same parity, so each class can be arranged freely
Fill each position from its own parity class
Build the number digit by digit
Position `i` must hold an odd digit iff the original digit there was odd
Parity of each position is fixed

p: `num = 1234`: odd digits sorted descending `[3, 1]`, even digits `[4, 2]`.

blocks.h: Why is greedy per class optimal?
p: Within a parity class any arrangement is reachable by swaps, and positions of the two classes don't interact. The largest number puts the biggest digit of each class at the leftmost position of that class. Making an earlier position larger always beats anything later, so sorting each class descending is optimal.

bullets: Time: O(d log d) for d digits.

2231.takeaway: Largest number after parity-preserving swaps: sort odd digits and even digits separately in descending order and refill the original parity pattern.
